newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Japan repels Taiwan, HK boats at disputed isles.
newsitem.headline: Japan repels Taiwan, HK boats at disputed isles.

text.p: Japanese patrol ships on Monday repelled five boats carrying Taiwan and Hong Kong activists trying to land on a disputed East China Sea archipelago, reports from the flotilla said.
State-run Taiwan Radio said two of the private boats "tried to force their way at full speed to the Diaoyu islands but were stopped by Japanese police vessels" just offshore.
"They are returning to Taiwan now because the Japanese force is really big," the radio said, putting the number of Japanese coast guard and police vessels at 17.

The five vessels carrying about 70 activists and journalists had set out to challenge Japan's claim of sovereignty to the uninhabited islands, known to the Japanese as the Senkakus and the Chinese as the Diaoyus.
Another protest vessel set sail for the islands from Hong Kong on Sunday.
A makeshift lighthouse built on one of the islands in July by a Japanese ultra-nationalist group has rekindled a festering dispute over the islands, claimed by Beijing, Taipei and Tokyo.
Pilots aborted the landing due to the overwhelming Japanese force as well as rough seas and a rocky shoreline, a Taiwan Television reporter told her station by ship-to-shore radio.
"We headed for the Diaoyu islands until we were only 100 metres (yards) away. We could see the lighthouse and the Japanese flag," she said. "Everyone was very emotional."
The activists had vowed to remove the lighthouse and flag.

The Taiwan group had hoped to plant the flag of the island's exiled Republic of China while the protesters from Hong Kong, a British colony which reverts to Chinese rule next year, carried that of the communist mainland's People's Republic of China.
There were no reports of violence or physical contact.

Japan's coast guard, asked for confirmation, said there had been "no trouble or conflict" but that it was duty-bound to "issue warnings and ask foreign ships to move out of Japan's territorial waters".
"There is no change in our response (to foreign ships)," a coast guard spokesman told Reuters by telephone from southern Okinawa, which has jurisdiction over the islands.
Taiwan radio said Japanese crewmen ignored the activists' demand to "Get out of Chinese territory!" and ordered the Taiwan ships to leave what they called Japanese territory.
Taiwan activists said they would not give up.
"We are confident that next time we will succeed," Taipei county assemblyman and protest organiser Chin Chieh-shou told the radio, pledging another attempt in late October.
Chinese anger swelled in Taiwan, Hong Kong, Macau and the communist mainland after Japanese patrol ships frustrated earlier Taiwanese attempts to approach the islands.

On Sunday, thousands of drum-beating demonstrators chanted "Down with Japanese militarism" and "Protect the Diaoyus" as they marched through Taipei streets, the latest in a series of anti-Japanese protests in Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau.
An effigy of Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto was tied to a car and flogged during the march.
Taiwan pledged on Saturday to defend the Diaoyus by force, but only as a last resort.
Japan has claimed sovereign rights to the islands and refused to acknowledge that the dispute is still open for discussion with China.

Tokyo's claim dates to 1895, when Japan defeated China and seized Taiwan and other territories. Beijing and Taipei say Chinese claims go back centuries but both have resisted calls to expel Japan by force.
Taiwan and China have been bitter rivals since a civil war split them in 1949 and the Republic of China government, defeated by the communists, took refuge on Taiwan.
